PID Speed Control of a Simulated DC Motor¶

Manish Dahal, Kathmandu University Robotics Club, Track 8

Objective: I simulated a motor whose speed is controlled by a PID controller. I tested what each setting does, tuned it with a standard recipe, made the simulated motor behave like a real one, and fixed a real-world problem.

AI tools helped me write the simulation code. I ran every test, checked the outputs, and wrote the explanations myself.

1. The motor¶

The motor does not reach full speed instantly. In my model it reaches 63% of its final speed after 0.5 seconds (the time constant). Its final speed equals the input, so the gain is 1.

2. Proportional (Kp):¶

Raising Kp from 1 to 20 cut the rise time from 0.550 s to 0.050 s. The final gap to the target shrank from 0.500 to 0.048 but never reached zero, because the push weakens as the gap closes.

3. Integral (Ki):¶

Adding Ki brought the final gap to zero. Raising Ki from 10 to 100 raised overshoot from 0% to 30.8%, because the controller kept pushing past the target while it paid off its stored memory.

4. Derivative (Kd):¶

With Kd added to the PID, overshoot fell from 19.4% to 15.6%, but settling time grew from 0.490 s to 0.915 s. Kd trims overshoot at the cost of speed. It does not remove the final gap (it stayed at 0.167 in the PD case).

5. Tuning Recipe (Ziegler-Nichols)¶

Ziegler-Nichols converts two motor measurements (delay and response speed) into PID gains. My measured delay was 0.05 s and response time was 0.522 s, giving Kp = 12.58, Ki = 126.31, and Kd = 0.313. It rose faster than my manual settings (0.060 s vs. 0.096 s) but produced higher overshoot (79.1% vs. 4.1%). The method prioritizes fast response and accepts larger overshoot to achieve it.

6. A more realistic motor¶

Real motors have limits. I added: a maximum voltage of 12 V (saturation), a dead zone of 1.5 V where nothing moves, friction, a coarse speed sensor, sensor noise, and a 10 ms delay. I checked the simulation by switching every effect off and confirming it matched the ideal model.

7. What each real-world effect does¶

Effect What changed in the curve Metric that changed Reason
Deadband (11 V) Speed hunts around the setpoint Settling 0.37 to 2.99 s, overshoot 2.0% The motor ignores outputs below 11 V, so the integral must overshoot to get movement.
Friction (2, P only) Final speed stops lower Final 8.33 to 8.00 Friction removes constant drive, and P alone cannot restore it. Ki can, as the PI run showed.
Saturation (12 V) Slow rise, then overshoot Overshoot 14.5%, settling 2.70 s Output is clipped while the integral keeps growing (windup).
Quantization (0.5) Final value stops short of the setpoint SSE 0.025 The encoder rounds 9.75 up to 10, so the integral stops growing.
Noise (0.2) Small jitter Overshoot 1.0%, settling 0.51 s Noise pushes the response outside the 2% band.
Delay (high gains) Much more oscillation Overshoot 10.9% to 33.0% One sample of delay lowers the stability margin at high gains.

Saturation rows are judged by final value and overshoot, because rise and settling times depend on the final value.

8. Fixing Windup (Anti-Windup)¶

While voltage sat at its upper limit, integral windup kept building up. Once the motor reached the target, that stored push caused overshoot. Clamping stops integral growth during output saturation. Overshoot dropped from 14.5% to 0.0%, and settling time dropped from 2.70 s to 1.60 s.

9. Findings¶

Higher Kp speeds up response but leaves steady-state error. Adding Ki removes steady-state error but increases overshoot (30.8% at Ki = 100).

Non-ideal effects change real behavior. Adding delay raised overshoot from 10.9% to 33.0%.

Clamping anti-windup reduced overshoot from 14.5% to 0.0%.

10. Limitations¶

  • The motor values (time constant, dead zone, friction) are assumed, not measured from a real motor.
  • Friction is simplified to a constant loss of push.
  • Everything is simulated, with no hardware test.
  • I chose the settings by hand, so I tested a small number of cases.
